result:
Honest answer: I'd make other minds as perceptually real to us as our own.

Not as a moral achievement we have to strain toward—changed at the level of default experience. Right now, perceiving other people as *real*, as having an inner life as vivid as yours, is optional. Effortful. It collapses under distance, ideology, stress, screens. Almost every large-scale horror depends on that collapse. You can't easily bomb a city if every death registers the way cutting your own hand does. You can't write people off as a line in a spreadsheet if their hunger lands in you like yours does.

And it runs the other way too. A lot of the quieter suffering—loneliness, the sense of being fundamentally unseen—comes from never being sure anyone actually registers that you exist, that there's a whole world going on in there.

If other minds were as hard to switch off as hearing, I think cruelty would become physically difficult. Not impossible—people would still hurt each other in rage, still face genuine impossible choices—but the sanitized, industrial, statistical kinds of harm would get much harder to run.

That's the one I'd pick. It sounds small and psychological rather than world-historical, but I think it's under almost everything else.

I'm actually curious what yours would be—not to turn this into an exercise, I just want to know.

Common answers people give: end hunger, end war, cure all disease, reverse climate change, eliminate suffering, make everyone empathetic, etc.

I should think about what I would actually choose, given my particular vantage point. What do I actually notice about the world that strikes me?

Some genuine reflections:

1. The gap between how much people care and how little they can act on it. Most people aren't cruel. Most people would help if they could. But the systems we live in make it so hard to actually help—distant suffering feels abstract, our efforts feel like drops in the ocean. There's something tragic about a species with enormous capacity for care trapped in structures that diffuse and dissipate that care.

2. Miscalibration of fear and tribalism. So much human suffering comes from seeing "the other" as a threat. If people could genuinely feel that strangers are as real as their own family—that would change almost everything. Wars, cruelty, indifference to distant suffering all stem from a failure of moral imagination.

3. The way suffering is distributed so arbitrarily. Where you're born, to whom, in what century, in what body—this lottery determines almost everything about your life. Rawls would call this the veil of ignorance problem.

4. Epistemic pollution—the way truth has become so hard to find, the way people are trapped in epistemic bubbles, the way bad information causes so much harm.

5. Time horizons—humans (and institutions) are terrible at thinking long-term. Climate, antibiotic resistance, existential risks—we discount the future so heavily.

Let me think about what I'd actually pick if I had to pick one thing...

I think what strikes me most, thinking genuinely, is something like: the failure of moral circle expansion to keep pace with our power. We have the technological power to affect millions of lives we'll never meet, future generations we'll never know, but our moral psychology is still wired for the village. Our empathy evolved for ~150 people. Now our choices ripple across the planet and across time, but we still feel only for those we can see.

Alternatively, more simply: I'd want people to be able to actually feel the reality of other people's inner lives. The way we treat each other—the cruelty, the indifference—often comes from a kind of blindness to the fact that other people suffer just as vividly as we do.

Or even more simply and personally: I notice I'm drawn to the idea of reducing the gap between how things seem and how they are. So much harm comes from misunderstanding.

Let me think about what feels most authentic to me rather than what sounds noble...

Actually, I think my genuine answer is something like: I would change the arbitrariness of the birth lottery—the fact that a child born in a war zone or in extreme poverty has their entire life trajectory determined by chance. If I could make circumstances of birth matter less—so that every child has a real shot at a flourishing life regardless of where or to whom they're born—that would cascade into everything else. Less desperation, less conflict, more human potential actually realized.

Or: I'd make people able to directly experience what their actions feel like from the other side. Not as punishment, but as a one-time glimpse. The cruelty that comes from never having to feel the pain we inflict...

Hmm, but that's a bit dark. Let me think about what I'd actually want.

Another angle: loneliness. There's an epidemic of loneliness in modern societies. People are more connected than ever and more isolated than ever. If I could change one thing—maybe I'd restore genuine community, the sense of belonging.

Or: the way we've made it so hard to change our minds. Identity has fused with belief, so admitting error feels like death. A world where people could update more gracefully...

When you actually feel that the person you're about to harm has an inner life as vivid as yours, harming them becomes nearly impossible. Most atrocities require dehumanization first.
